metadata.title: It Never Says Pass
metadata.note: cli-explainer spine, weekly work report, claude-hai channel. Episode 4, finale of the six-step arc. Built to the PROOF rubric — FRAMEWORK (three questions for any automated report: WHAT A RECORD SUPPORTS / WHAT YOU INFERRED / WHO DECIDES) shown before any example, step 6 scored on it, and a falsifiability beat the framework PREDICTS that calls back to episode 1 (gate 4 is satisfiable by doing nothing — a gate with nothing to fail). Title taken verbatim from the script's own rule. Every figure from a live run — see SOURCES.md / FACTCHECK.md.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name. HAI short-form greeting.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane, and this is my week on Mycroft. Step six is written, which means all six now exist. And the last one's whole job is to not reach a conclusion.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the week's ask, answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the week's ask and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "write step 6: turn the prior five steps' output into a report a human can decide from"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · It Never Says Pass

beats.role_note: series continuity — the ledger completes. Kept tight so the FRAMEWORK lands near ~20s.
beats.narration_text: Three episodes ago this recipe had six steps and none of them were implemented. Step six is the report — the thing that turns everything the machine found into a decision a human can actually make. Writing it raised the question the whole series has been circling.
beats.new_visual_element: the six-step ledger, the last row closing

shot.show: the six recipe steps, five already done, the sixth closing
shot.visual_intent: The same six-row ledger used in every episode. Steps 1-5 already ink with ticks. Step 6 resolves from terracotta to ink and gains its tick — the arc completing on screen. The shape is deliberately unchanged from episodes 1 through 3.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions for any automated report, shown AS A STRUCTURE before the step is examined
beats.narration_text: Three questions for any automated report. One: what does a record actually support? Two: what did you infer — arithmetic, a model, a judgment? Three: who decides? Most reporting tools blur one and two, and then quietly answer three themselves. This one refuses to.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT A RECORD SUPPORTS / WHAT YOU INFERRED / WHO DECIDES
shot.visual_intent: Three cards land in a row, one per narration step. They stay on screen as the rubric the rest of the reel is scored against; the third is the one the gates answer.

beats.role_note: cycle 1 ask — SPARK-LINE LAW: greeting is the spark line
beats.narration_text: So, step six. Read everything the prior five steps produced, and write the report. Fifteen sections the output contract requires, a machine log alongside it, and an audit written beside the data it inspects.

shot.show: the Claude composer carrying the step-6 prompt

props.command: claude "write step 6: the human report, the agent log, and an audit beside the data — all from one pass over the evidence"
output: every number carries its trace chain
each artifact records its own sha256

beats.role_note: THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the rule the episode is named for, verbatim
beats.narration_text: And here is the rule it is built on. Verified findings are only what a record supports — counts, hashes, defect locators, gate evidence. The sentiment score is not one of those. It is arithmetic over a keyword count with unattributed weights, so it goes under inferred findings, with its flags attached. Then the last line: an audit reports what it found. It never says pass.
beats.new_visual_element: the VERIFIED VERSUS INFERRED rule, verbatim

props.title: scripts/tools/...-produce-human-report.py
props.code:
VERIFIED VERSUS INFERRED (P3, P8):
    The sentiment score is an INFERRED finding. It is arithmetic
    over a keyword count with unattributed weights, not a market
    observation, and it appears under "Inferred findings" with
    its flags attached.

    Verified findings are only what a record supports: counts,
    hashes, defect locators, gate evidence.

    An audit reports what it found; it never says "pass".

beats.role_note: cycle 1 output — the findings split, live. Callback to episode 3's 64.
beats.narration_text: Run it on the corrupted set and the split is visible. Ten verified findings: rows seen, rows promoted, rows withheld on shape, and the envelope that declared seven records while holding eight. Five inferred: every component score, and the overall sixty-four. That is the same sixty-four from last episode — the one that could not tell clean data from corrupted. It is not a verified finding. It never was.

shot.show: two columns — 10 verified findings against 5 inferred, with the 64 sitting on the inferred side
shot.visual_intent: Two panels held side by side. VERIFIED, in ink: counts, rows withheld, the envelope discrepancy. INFERRED, in terracotta: the component scores and the overall 64. The 64 sitting on the terracotta side is the beat — it is the number the previous episode chased.

beats.role_note: THE REVISION LAW — cycle 2, the gates
beats.narration_text: Then the gates. Six of them, each with a human capacity named in the recipe. And the tempting thing — the thing almost every pipeline does — is to mark them green once the checks come back clean.

shot.show: the Claude composer carrying the gates prompt

props.command: claude "report each gate's evidence and blocking findings — and do not mark any of them passed"
output: cleared_by: null — awaiting a named human

beats.role_note: THE ACTUAL-CODE LAW — the two-customers rule and the reader it targets, verbatim
beats.narration_text: It writes both artifacts from one pass, so they can never disagree — a J S O N log for agents, a markdown report for humans, and the report's numbers read from the same dictionary the log serialises. And it targets the stricter reader: every number carries its trace chain back to a raw locator and a source hash, and each artifact records its own S H A two five six, so a reviewer can prove the file they are reading is the one the report cites.

props.title: scripts/tools/...-produce-human-report.py
props.code:
TWO CUSTOMERS, TWICE (P5):
    The same run produces a JSON log for agents and a Markdown
    report for humans. One artifact cannot serve both, so this
    step writes both from one pass over the evidence and never
    lets them disagree -- the report's numbers are read from the
    same dict the log serialises.

THE REPORT'S READER:
    ... someone who must reconstruct exactly how any score was
    produced. Every number carries its trace chain
    (score -> contributing rows -> verified file -> raw locator
     -> raw source path + SHA-256).
props.sparkLine: One pass, two readers, no disagreement

beats.role_note: cycle 2 output — the centrepiece: six gates, none passed. Live run.
beats.narration_text: Fifteen of fifteen sections present. Sixteen of sixteen required log fields. Six gates. And every single one of them reads: evidence recorded, awaiting a named human. Not one marked passed. The report and the audit are byte-identical across reruns; the log differs in exactly one field, the timestamp the contract requires. And no-write creates nothing at all.
beats.new_visual_element: six gate rows, all awaiting a human

shot.show: six gate rows each reading 'evidence recorded; awaiting a named human', with the contract counts above
shot.visual_intent: Counts land first: 15/15 sections, 16/16 log fields. Then six gate rows resolve one at a time, every one carrying the same terracotta status chip — awaiting a named human. The repetition is the point: no green anywhere.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — the defect the report caught in ITSELF, and a direct callback to episode 1
beats.narration_text: Now the one it caught on itself. Gate four is the script-readiness gate. Its condition: every step script exists, or is represented by a typed development to-do. Read that again. It passes if the script exists — or if the to-do text is still sitting in the recipe. Both are currently true. It is satisfiable by doing nothing. And the report prints that sentence rather than quietly recording a pass. Episode one said a validator with nothing to catch is not passing. This is a gate with nothing to fail.
beats.new_visual_element: the gate condition, and why it cannot fail

shot.show: gate 4's condition split into its two branches, both currently true
shot.visual_intent: The gate condition sits at the top. Beneath it, two branches drawn side by side: 'the script exists' and 'the TODO text is still in the recipe'. Both resolve to TRUE in terracotta, held together. The verdict beneath: satisfiable by doing nothing.

beats.role_note: the series ledger closes — what is done and what is deliberately not
beats.narration_text: So the ledger closes. Six of six steps written, running end to end on both fixture sets. All six gate tests check out. Gate five still has no approval record, so live and model execution stay blocked. And nine typed to-dos are carried forward — including a reader mismatch the step logged rather than editing the recipe to hide.
beats.new_visual_element: the closing ledger — done versus deliberately open

shot.show: two-column ledger: complete versus deliberately open, with the commit named
shot.visual_intent: Left column fills in ink: 6 of 6 steps, both fixture sets, all six gate tests, byte-identical reruns. Right column in terracotta: gate 5 unapproved so live execution blocked, 9 typed TODOs carried. Kicker names commit aa0c0fe.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW + PROOF active-task rule — question 3 turned on the viewer, with a good/bad discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn, and it is question three. Find a dashboard or a report your team trusts. Paste this. For every green indicator on it, tell me what condition would make it red, and whether anything in the last ninety days actually made it red. A good answer names a failing condition and the last time it fired. A bad answer tells you everything is healthy — which is exactly what a gate that cannot fail also says.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the handoff prompt typed in

shot.show: the Claude composer with the viewer's prompt and the good/bad test

props.command: claude "for every green indicator on this dashboard: what condition turns it red, and when did it last actually turn red?"
output: GOOD: a failing condition + when it last fired
a check that cannot fail is not a check
